title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
section: The Problem with a Blank Prompt
text:
The Problem with a Blank Prompt

Earlier today: the brain has amnesia — it only knows what’s on the desk.



So put the right sources on the desk — and make it answer from those only.









The goal


Without grounding in real sources, even the smartest brain will guess.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Wrong Way vs. Right Way



Wrong
“Summarize the literature on active learning.”
→ Generic, maybe fabricated citations.



Right
Upload 5 papers → “Based only on these, summarize…”
→ Specific, citable, defensible.




No upload = no trust. Context comes before content.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
The Golden Rule

If it doesn’t have a citation, it didn’t happen.



For research, teaching materials, and committee work — demand the page reference.

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
What It’s Best At

Deep reading of big documents (50+ pages). It builds a guide solely from your uploaded sources — no internet guessing — and every answer links back to the source.



Upload papers, a thesis, a policy, lecture readings
Ask questions; get answers with citations to the exact passage
Generate an Audio Overview to listen on your commute

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM

title: Grounding & Creating with NotebookLM
text:
Steering & Editing the Deck

Before generating: name your audience, emphasize themes, or structure it around specific questions
Export straight to .pptx — editable PowerPoint
Revise any slide: a pencil icon → type how to change the wording, emphasis, or visual








One requirement


You need at least one source uploaded before it can build a deck — grounding first, always.

Take a real (safe) paper or policy PDF. Produce a 1-page grounded summary and a presenter deck — in 10 minutes.

10 minutes vs. the hours it used to take. That’s the number for the Wrap-up.

A Chat Box

You paste, it replies
One message at a time

Same brain in the jar. A much more capable office around it.

Skill
A book in your library, opened by name

Code it writes & runs to compute exactly





All three turn a one-time effort into a permanent capability.

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
What a Skill Is

Your Skills are a library. Each Skill is a book — a written playbook for one recurring task.



Cowork keeps the whole shelf, but only opens the book your task calls for — not every book, every time. (just like the office puts only the relevant page on the desk)




The title on the spine — the trigger that tells Cowork which book to pull
What’s written inside — the steps, in plain language

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:

Lecture notes → an on-brand revealjs slide deck you open in your browser.



Name: Lecture Deck  •  Trigger: “turn these notes into a revealjs deck”
Steps: 1) outline the storyline · 2) one idea per slide · 3) apply my course style · 4) generate a revealjs file with a Quarto front-matter

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
Invoke It on Fresh Input

“Turn this into a lecture deck: photosynthesis — light reactions, Calvin cycle, limiting factors, today’s lab.”



One phrase → a browser-ready deck. No re-explaining.

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
What a Script Is

A little program Cowork writes and runs when the job is exact, repeatable calculation — math and data done the same way every single time.



The brain in a jar estimates — and can slip on arithmetic. A computer computes the same way every time. So Cowork doesn’t do the math in its head — it writes a script.









You still never touch code


This is Session 2’s “repeatable steps, every time” — now done as real code. You never write or even see it: you describe what you want, Cowork writes and runs the script, you get the result.

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
Demo 2 — Grade Summaries

You have a spreadsheet of raw scores. You want weighted finals, the class average, and a distribution — every term.



“From grades.csv, compute each student’s weighted total (midterm 25%, final 35%, project 25%, participation 15%), the class average, and a grade distribution. Save it as a new sheet.”







Note


Sample data: grades.csv

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
Why a Script Here

Exact, every row — the script computes, it doesn’t estimate
Reproducible next term — same script, same method; no formula errors, no copy-paste
You get the result, not the code — describe it once, Cowork writes and runs it








Pair it with “double-check”


For anything graded, ask it to compute twice and compare before you trust the numbers.

title: Meet Claude Cowork & Automating Your Work
text:
A Standing Appointment

Type /schedule in any Cowork task. “Every Sunday at 5pm, draft my week-ahead teaching summary.” It just happens — you didn’t have to ask.



The leap from a tool you operate to a teammate that acts on its own.

/schedule: Every Sunday 5pm — scan the course folder and draft a summary of what’s due, ungraded, and upcoming. Notify me; don’t send anything.

Every scheduled job starts in draft / notify-me mode. Promote to act-on-its-own only after you’ve watched it get it right.

A notebook where the office jots down lasting facts about you — your role, your preferences, your recurring projects — and flips back to it on future visits.

The difference between a temp and an assistant who’s worked with you for a year.

title: Memory
section: Rules You Set vs. Facts It Keeps
text:
Rules You Set vs. Facts It Keeps




CLAUDE.md — the wall note
Rules you set on purpose.
Per Project.





Memory — the notebook
Facts the agent accumulates about you.
Across Projects.










Rule of thumb


A standing rule for one project → CLAUDE.md. A fact about you that’s true everywhere → Memory.

title: Memory
text:
Set It Once
Seed Memory with your defaults so the agent always sounds like you, not a robot — across every Project:

Role — who you are and what you do
Tone — how you write (concise, warm, direct…)
Format — your go-to structure (BLUF, bullets, headers)








The payoff


A new Project still starts in your voice — no setup, no reminding.

title: Memory
text:
Hands-On






Steps



Seed Memory with your working style + a few standing facts.
Start a fresh session.
Ask for something — confirm it carries your style over with zero reminders.






That carry-over is the office re-sending the right pages (Session 2).

title: Memory
text:
Keep the Notebook Clean

Memory gets re-sent to the brain. So the Newspaper Test applies here too.








Nothing in the notebook…


…that you wouldn’t want re-sent. Keep it sanitized — no secrets, no raw PII.

title: Memory

Memory = the notebook — persistent facts about you, across sessions

Default persona — set Role, Tone, Format once; sound like you everywhere
It’s still context — keep Memory sanitized; nothing you wouldn’t want re-sent
One-off details — belong in the message, not the notebook

text:

Session 2: The model has amnesia — it only knows what’s on the desk.

title: Grounding AI in Truth
text:
The Wrong Way

Open AI → Type question → Hope for the best



“Write a report on the Saudi Fintech market.”
→ Generic, Wikipedia-style summary from 2021.

title: Grounding AI in Truth

Upload source → Give instructions → Get grounded results



Upload the SAMA Financial Sector Report → “Based only on this report, summarize…”

Don’t ask — “What are the trends in tourism?”

The Rule


No upload = no trust. Context comes before content.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Session 1 Left a Question

AI predicts the next word. It doesn’t “know” facts.



So how does it ever feel like it remembers you?









Today’s keystone


Everything else in this course hangs off one insight: you’re really talking to two layers stacked together.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Two Layers, Stacked




The Model Layer
“The brain in a jar”





The App Layer
“The office around the brain”





Tell these apart and CLAUDE.md, Projects, Memory, and Skills stop being magic.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
A Brilliant Brain — With Amnesia

A brilliant graduate’s brain floating in a jar. It has read most of the internet, so it’s clever — but it has total amnesia.



Knows nothing about you, your company, or what you said five minutes ago
The instant it finishes answering, it forgets everything
All it does is predict the next word from the text it was just handed

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
What It Really Is

The model is stateless. It does not “remember” and it does not “look things up”.








The same prediction engine from Session 1


When it doesn’t know, it predicts a plausible-sounding word anyway — that’s a hallucination.






Anything you want it to “know”, you must hand it every single time.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
We Build an Office

The brain in a jar can’t open files or remember your name. So we build an office around it: filing cabinets, a notebook, a standing to-do list.


Every time you ask for something, the office gathers the relevant pages and hands them to the brain along with your request — then files the answer back.



The brain still has amnesia. The office is what makes it feel like it remembers.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
What It Really Is

The app (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, the Hermes agent…) is the software wrapped around the model.


It stores your information in files / a directory and re-sends the relevant parts on every request.








The features you’ve seen


“Memory”, “Projects”, “Custom Instructions” are all just the app doing this gathering-and-resending for you.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
The Sentence to Remember

The model knows nothing and forgets everything; the app re-sends what matters on every request.



Every feature in this course is just the app getting smarter about what to re-send.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Context = the Desk

Context is everything the office stacks on the brain’s desk before it starts — your request plus the background pages it needs to do the job well.


Your instructions, pasted documents, standing rules, relevant memory — the model’s entire world for that one request.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
The Big Reframe

Output quality is mostly a context problem, not a smartness problem.








What this means for you


A weak answer usually means weak context, not a weak model. “Give it context” is the whole skill.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Why Long Chats “Forget”

The brain’s desk has a fixed size. You can only fit so many pages on it at once. Pile on too much and older pages fall off the edge.



That’s the context window — and it’s why a long conversation starts losing the thread from the beginning.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
The Payoff: Saved Beats Re-Pasted






The rule


Saved instructions beat re-pasting.



The app puts the important pages back on the desk for you every time, so they never fall off the edge.


This is the entire reason CLAUDE.md, Projects, and Memory exist — coming on Day 2.

title: How AI Actually Works
section: A Script Is Saved, Repeatable Steps
text:
A Script Is Saved, Repeatable Steps

Saved steps, written down once, so the job runs the same way every time — exact, down to the last row.








Not a programmer thing


A “script” is just “do these exact steps, in this order, every time.” For precise work, the agent writes and runs it as real code — you never write, or even see, code in this course. You describe what you want; you get the result.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
The Office Getting Smarter
Once you see the two layers, the whole Day-2 toolkit is just the app deciding what to re-send:

CLAUDE.md — standing instructions, re-sent every time
Project — pulls the right folder’s pages onto the desk
Memory — facts about you, re-sent when relevant
Skill — a book in the library the app opens on command



None of it is magic. It’s all context management.

title: How AI Actually Works
section: Write the Pages the Brain Needs
text:
Write the Pages the Brain Needs
Pick one task from your Automation Backlog (Session 1). Write its context pack — the standing facts the AI would need every single time to do it well:

Who you are and your role
The tone and format you always want
The rules that never change (audience, do’s and don’ts)
The background facts the task always assumes








Keep it


On Day 2 this becomes your first CLAUDE.md — paste it once, never re-type it again.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Quiz — Question 1
The AI gets the tone wrong every single time — too casual for your board.
Which layer?



The App Layer — fix your standing instructions. It’s a re-send problem, not the brain.

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Quiz — Question 2
The AI cites “Article 214” of a law — and the article doesn’t exist.
Which layer?



The Model Layer — the brain guessed. Ground it in a real source and verify (Session 4).

title: How AI Actually Works
text:
Key Takeaways

Two layers — the model (brain) and the app (office) stacked together
The brain has amnesia — stateless, predicts the next word, forgets everything
The office re-sends context — that’s what makes AI feel like it remembers
Quality is a context problem — give it the right pages, get the right answer
The desk is finite — saved instructions beat re-pasting
Day 2 = the office getting smarter about what to re-send

Package Your Best Work

Bundle your best Skills so a teammate could run them tomorrow — your own library of books.








The real habit


Reach for the library at each bottleneck — instead of solving the same task from scratch, again.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
The Problem

It’s not the design. It’s the story.



Too much text
No clear argument
“Frankenstein” decks (pasted from 5 different files)

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
The Amazon Method

Amazon banned PowerPoint in meetings.



Narrative First. Design Second.



Writing the memo forces you to think. Slides let you hide.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
The Move

Ask the AI to “think step by step” or “show your work” before giving the answer.








Why?


It drastically reduces hallucinations and improves logic. (Session 3’s first advanced move — now applied to a story.)

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
The Narrative Workflow

1. The Brain Dump

Paste raw context (notes, goals).


2. The Narrative (The Pitch)

AI writes a 1-page memo.



3. The Roast (The Stress Test)

AI acts as a skeptical CFO and finds holes in the logic.



4. The Blueprint

Convert the refined memo into a slide outline.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Step 1: The Narrative Prompt

Role: You represent the Project Lead.
Instructions: Write a 1-page “Amazon Style” narrative memo pitching [Project X].
Context: - Goal: Get $50k budget approved - Problem: Current system is too slow - Solution: Implement Tool Z
Constraint: Be concise, brutal, and data-driven. No fluff.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Step 2: The Roast

Crucial Step



Role: You are the skeptical CFO.
Instructions: Roast this memo. Find the holes in the logic. Where is the ROI unclear? What risks are missing? Be harsh.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Step 3: The Blueprint
Once the logic is solid, turn text into visuals.

Task: Convert the narrative into a 5-slide outline.
Format: - Slide Title: (action-oriented) - The Hook: (one-sentence summary) - Visual: (describe the EXACT chart — e.g. “Bar chart showing 20% growth”, NOT “a picture of growth”) - Speaker Notes: (bullet points)

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Two Routes




Method A — One-Click
Gamma: paste the outline → generate a full deck.
Fast, modern, great for internal use.





Method B — Corporate-Safe
Word / Markdown → PowerPoint: outline into your official template.
Zero manual formatting, on-brand.










Same blueprint, either engine


Your “Visual” descriptors from Step 3 are the fuel — they tell the engine exactly what each slide shows.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Your Mission

From raw crisis notes, produce a roasted narrative and a 5-slide on-brand deck — before the meeting starts.



Draft — AI writes the 1-page argument
Roast — AI tears it apart; you fix the logic
Blueprint — 5-slide outline with visual descriptors
Design Engine — outline → finished deck (Gamma or template)









Log it


Record the time vs. building the deck by hand. Have a real pitch you owe someone? Run that.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Quiz
Question: Why do we write the narrative before we open the design engine?


1. Because AI likes memos.




2. Because the story is the hard part — and a roasted argument makes every later slide stronger.





3. Design is cheap once the logic is solid — the engine just dresses a sound argument.

title: From Notes to Narrative
text:
Key Takeaways

Story before slides — never open the design tool first
Think step by step — use AI to think, not just write
The Roast — let the AI be your harshest critic
The Blueprint — visual descriptors are the fuel for the engine
The Design Engine — Gamma (one-click) or template (corporate-safe) finishes the deck

title: Interviewing Your Data
section: The Old Way vs. The New Way
text:
The Old Way vs. The New Way




Old way
VLOOKUP, pivot tables, formulas, hours of wrangling.





New way
Upload the file. Ask in plain language.





You hand the agent the spreadsheet (the desk), then interview it.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Questions, Not Formulas
Upload expenses_export.csv and ask:

“What is our fastest-growing expense category?”
“Summarize the spending trends for Q3 vs. Q2.”
“Which vendor did we spend the most with — and on what?”
“Flag any expense that looks like a duplicate or an outlier.”








The skill is the question


A precise question gets a precise answer. Vague in, vague out.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Read a Receipt, Reconcile It

Hand the agent a receipt image → it pulls out vendor, date, amount, VAT (OCR) → then reconciles it against the expense export.



“Does this receipt match a row in the file? If not, add it.”









Verify the numbers


A great moment for double-check (Session 3) — totals are expensive to get wrong.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Plan on the Enriched Data

“If we cut Travel by 20%, what’s the new monthly total?”
“What’s the VAT impact if Meals doubles next quarter?”
“Which two categories would I trim to save 10,000 SAR?”








Newspaper Test still applies


Real financials? Sanitize or use the sandbox dataset before uploading.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Run a Real Interview






Hands-on


Open hermes-agent-course/data/expenses_export.csv in the agent and run an interview: ask 3 questions, extract one receipt, and model one “what-if”.





Log the time vs. building the formulas by hand.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Quiz
Which question will get the most useful answer?





A) “Tell me about the expenses.”
❌ Too vague — you’ll get a shrug.





B) “Top 3 categories by total spend, with the % each is of the month.”
✅ Specific metric, grouping, and format.

title: Interviewing Your Data
text:
Key Takeaways

Interview, don’t formula — upload the file and ask in plain language
Precise questions win — name the metric, the grouping, the format
Extract & enrich — OCR a receipt, then reconcile against the data
“What if” on the spot — model budget changes conversationally
Verify & sanitize — double-check the numbers; mind the Newspaper Test

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
How Most People Use AI

Ask a question → Get an answer


This is the Search Mindset — and it wastes 90% of AI’s value.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
The Partner Mindset

Give context → Iterate together → Get real results



Treat the AI like a smart intern who needs context, instruction, and feedback.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Example: Client Delay Email

Search Mindset:
“Write an email to a client about a delay.”


Result: Generic, robotic, sounds fake.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Example: Client Delay Email

Partner Mindset:
“I need to email Client X about a 3-day delay — we’re waiting for final internal approval. Tone: respectful but confident. Here is the project context…”


Result: Tailored, professional — sounds like you.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
section: Trap 1: Generally treating it like Search
text:
Trap 1: Generally treating it like Search

The Input Mistake
Asking short questions like a Google search.








The Fix: Better Inputs


Shift from Querying to Conversing. Give context.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
section: Trap 2: Treating It Like a Person
text:
Trap 2: Treating It Like a Person

The Interaction Mistake

“Please,” “Thank you,” “I’m sorry to bother you…”









The Fix: Direct Commands


Be direct. Clear commands > polite requests. Validate output, don’t compliment it.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Trap 3: Over-trusting

The Output Mistake
Assuming AI contains facts like a database.



Reality: AI is a Prediction Engine — it guesses the next word. It does not “know” facts.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
How It Actually Works

The AI predicts the next word based on probability.

“The capital of Saudi Arabia is…”



Riyadh (99.8%) ✅




Jeddah (0.1%)




Paris (0.00001%)




It doesn’t “know” geography. It knows that “Riyadh” almost always follows that sentence.








Hold that thought


Why it predicts instead of knows — and what that means for everything you build — is the keystone of Session 2.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
When It Guesses Wrong (Hallucinations)

What happens when it doesn’t know the answer? It guesses.

“According to Article 214 of the new Saudi Investment Law: …”



The (45%)
Foreign (30%)
Capital (15%)





The AI constructs a sentence that sounds legal, but it has never read the actual document.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Trust but Verify






The Rule


AI is a drafting tool, not a fact-checking tool.






Trust AI for:

Logic & structure
Drafting & writing
Brainstorming




Verify AI on:

Facts & dates
Math & calculations
Legal citations

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
The Bottleneck Test
Hand a task to AI when it is:



✅ Good fit

Repetitive & mundane — routine emails, status updates
Data-intensive — summarizing, finding patterns
Drafting & brainstorming — beating the blank page
Predictable — clear, logical steps




⚠️ Keep a human in the loop

High-stakes — ethics, safety, big consequences
Deeply human — empathy, relationships
Confidential — sensitive or proprietary data
Originality is the point — a truly unique take

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
The Newspaper Test

Before pasting anything into AI, ask:



“If this appeared on the front page of the New York Times, would I be fired or sued?”




Yes or Maybe → DO NOT PASTE IT.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
High-Risk Data






Never share with AI







PII — Names, National IDs (Iqama/Saudi ID), phone numbers
Financial secrets — Unreleased earnings, bank accounts, salary data
Trade secrets — Proprietary code, formulas, unreleased strategy docs

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Sanitization: 3 Steps
Remove the specifics, keep the structure.

Anonymize — “Mohammed Al-Salem” → “[Employee A]”
Generalize — “5,000,000 SAR” → “5M+ SAR”
Strip identifiers — Remove company names, project codes, addresses

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
Before: Unsafe

“Layla Al-Harbi missed her Q3 sales target of 1.5M SAR by 15%. She blamed the delay in the Riyadh Season Campaign launch.”


Names, amounts, projects — all exposed.

title: The AI-Native Mindset & Your Automation Backlog
text:
After: Sanitized

“[Employee] missed their quarterly sales target by 15%. They cited delays in [Key Project] launch as the primary reason.”


Now you can safely ask: “Draft constructive feedback for [Employee] based on this…”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
From Mental Model to Action

Session 2: How AI actually works — the two layers



Session 3: Putting the right context on the desk — on purpose

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The Paradigm Shift

Stop Chatting. Start Delegating.



You don’t need a “chat bot”. You need a Direct Report.




Don’t Ask: “Write an email about the meeting.”
Delegate: “Act as a Project Manager. Draft a recap email using these notes. Highlight action items.”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The Framework


R — Role: Who is the AI?


I — Instructions: What exactly should it do?


C — Context: What does it know?


E — Examples: Show it what “good” looks like.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
R — Role

Who should the AI be?



A Senior Consultant
A Python Expert
An Angry Customer
A Legal Compliance Officer



The role shapes the AI’s vocabulary, perspective, and priorities.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
I — Instructions

What exactly should it do?


Be specific — bundle the task with its format, length, and tone:


“Draft a 200-word executive summary email to the Director. Professional but warm. Use bold headers.”










Pro move


Add: “If anything is unclear, ask me before you write.”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
C — Context

What does it know?


The “brain dump” — paste your notes, upload your docs, give it the raw material.








This is the same context from Session 2


You are loading the pages onto the brain’s desk. No context = the brain guesses.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
E — Examples

Show it what “good” looks like.


Don’t just describe the output you want — paste one sample. The AI copies its structure, tone, and length.


“Match this style: ‘Hi [Name], great speaking Tuesday. Here’s where we landed: …’”










One example beats a paragraph


A single sample teaches more than ten lines of rules.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The Formula

“Act as a [Role]. Your job is to [Instructions]. Here is the [Context]. Match this [Example].”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The Story

I nearly lost an $18,000 deal because of seven words in a notebook:



“Follow up on the pricing stuff soon.”



3 days later — the client asked if I had forgotten her.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The Messy Notes

This is what I actually had:


“Meeting with Lisa from Acme Retail. Tuesday. She’s worried about lead times. Wants to know if we can ship by Q3. Pricing: she needs a 10% discount if they buy bulk. Mentioned her kid’s graduation is next week (send a card?). Action: send updated proposal by Friday.”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
The RICE Prompt

Role: Act as my Senior Client Relationship Manager.
Instructions: Draft a warm-but-professional follow-up email summarizing our conversation and confirming next steps. Use headers — Summary, Decisions, Next Steps. Highlight deadlines in bold. If details are missing, add a “Clarifications Needed” section.
Context: I just had a call with a VIP client, Lisa. We are negotiating a large contract. Here are my raw notes: [paste notes]
Example: Match this opening style — “Hi Lisa, great speaking with you on Tuesday. Here’s where we landed: …”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
What Made It Work

Role → knew to write as a relationship manager, not a robot
Instructions → specific deliverable + format, tone, and the “Clarifications” rule
Context → messy notes were enough — AI extracted the structure
Example → matched the warm opening, so it caught the human touch (graduation card)

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Fast vs. Right

By default, AI answers fast and shallow — and fast is sloppy on hard problems.








The Rule


Complex tasks need the slow answer. These 3 moves force the AI to slow down — or, use a thinking model that does it automatically.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Move 1 — Think Step by Step

Add “think step by step” — make the AI show its reasoning before the answer.


Industry term: Chain of Thought (CoT). Best for logic, math, scheduling.



“I have a 2-hour meeting from 11:00, with a 30-min lunch at 12:00. When does it end? Think step by step.” → It blocks each segment and lands on 1:30 PM, not 1:00.









2025 update — thinking models do this automatically


Thinking models (o3, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Claude 3.7 Sonnet…) run CoT internally before every reply. You don’t need to say it — but you do need to choose the right model for hard problems.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Move 2 — Debate It Out

Make the AI argue from several expert viewpoints, then synthesize.


Industry term: Tree of Thoughts (ToT). Best for strategy and judgment calls.



“Three experts debate the reply to an angry client — Empathetic Lead, Pragmatic PM, Legal Advisor. Have them argue, then synthesize one balanced response.”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Move 3 — Double-Check

Have the AI solve the same problem 3 times independently — match = trust, mismatch = flag.


Industry term: Self-Consistency. Best for numbers and data extraction.



“Sum these invoice line items 3 separate times. If all three match, output ‘Verified’; if not, ‘Manual Review Needed’.”

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Which Move, When?








Problem Type
Move
Why




Logic / Math / Scheduling
Think step by step (CoT)
Forces careful, ordered reasoning


Strategy / Judgment calls
Debate it out (ToT)
Explores multiple perspectives


Data Extraction / Numbers
Double-check (Self-Consistency)
Catches errors through repetition










You can combine them


Double-check a step-by-step result. Think step by step inside a debate.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Apply It to Real Work






Two-part build



Pick a “messy input → clean output” task from your Automation Backlog and write a full RICE delegation for it.
Pick a decision or calculation task and add the matching advanced move.






Run it. Refine it. Log the time saved in your Time Log.

title: Delegating to AI
text:
Quiz — Question 1
You prompt: “Write a marketing post about our new coffee shop in Riyadh.”
Which RICE elements are missing?





R — Role
Who is writing?



I — Instructions
Partial — platform? length? tone?



C — Context

text:

In Session 3 you wrote a great delegation — but you typed it out by hand.



A Skill turns that one-time delegation into a permanent capability you invoke on command — by name or a trigger phrase, never re-typed.

title: Skills

A Book in Your Library

A book on the office shelf. You say “make the quarterly summary” and the agent pulls that book and follows it — and only that one, not the whole shelf. You don’t re-explain the steps.


A Skill is just three things:

A name — what you call it
The title on the spine (the trigger) — the phrase that tells the agent which book to pull (e.g. “turn this into a deck”)
What’s written inside — the steps, in plain language









No code


You describe the steps in plain language. The agent does the rest — you never write any.

title: Skills
text:
Two Homes for a Rule



Standing Instruction — Session 6
A tone, format, or rule you want applied to every request. Pinned to the Project wall (CLAUDE.md) — always on, you never ask for it.



Skill — Session 7
A procedure you invoke for a specific job — often producing an artifact. You call it by name / trigger when you need it.




“Always write memos in our house voice” → standing instruction. “Turn these notes into a memo, now” → Skill you invoke.


Same capability — the test is whether it’s always-on or invoked on demand.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Why Start Here?

Understand how it works and you’ll know what to trust, what to check, and how to get better answers.



Everything else today hangs off one insight: you’re talking to two layers stacked together.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Two Layers, Stacked




The Model Layer
“The brain in a jar”





The App Layer
“The office around the brain”





Tell these apart and Cowork, Skills, and Memory stop being magic.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
A Brilliant Brain — With Amnesia

A brilliant graduate’s brain floating in a jar. It has read most of the internet, so it’s clever — but it has total amnesia.



Knows nothing about you, your department, or what you said five minutes ago
The instant it finishes answering, it forgets everything
All it does is predict the next word from the text it was just handed

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
section: It Just Predicts the Next Word
text:
It Just Predicts the Next Word
Under the hood it does one thing: guess the next word based on probability.

“The capital of Saudi Arabia is…”




Riyadh (99.8%) ✅




Jeddah (0.1%) · Paris (0.00001%)




It doesn’t “know” geography — it knows “Riyadh” almost always follows that sentence.



It does this even when it has no idea — the next slide.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
When It Guesses Wrong (Hallucinations)

What happens when it doesn’t know the answer? It guesses.

“According to Article 214 of the new Saudi Investment Law: …”



The (45%)
Foreign (30%)
Capital (15%)





The AI constructs a sentence that sounds legal, but it has never read the actual document.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Limit That Explains Everything

The model is stateless. It does not “remember” and it does not “look things up.”








This is why it “hallucinates”


When it doesn’t know, it predicts a plausible-sounding answer anyway — a confident, made-up citation, a journal that doesn’t exist, a wrong date.






Anything you want it to “know,” you must hand it every single time.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
We Build an Office

The brain in a jar can’t open files or remember your name. So we build an office around it: filing cabinets, a notebook, a standing to-do list.


Every time you ask for something, the office gathers the relevant pages and hands them to the brain along with your request — then files the answer back.



The brain still has amnesia. The office is what makes it feel like it remembers.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Sentence to Remember

The model knows nothing and forgets everything; the app re-sends what matters on every request.








The features you’ve seen


“Memory,” “Projects,” “Custom Instructions” are all just the app gathering and re-sending context for you. Cowork (later today) is a very capable office.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Context = the Desk

Context is everything stacked on the brain’s desk before it starts — your request plus the background pages it needs: your instructions, the paper you pasted, your rules.



Output quality is mostly a context problem, not a smartness problem.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Desk Has Limits

The desk has a fixed size. Pile on too much and older pages fall off the edge — that’s why a long chat starts forgetting how it began.








The fix


Saved instructions beat re-pasting. The office puts the important pages back on the desk for you every time — the foundation of the assistant you’ll build today.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Office Getting Smarter
Everything you’ll build today is just the app deciding what to re-send:

Standing instructions — your rules, re-sent every time
Memory — facts about you, re-sent when relevant
Skill — a book in the library the app opens on command
Grounding — your sources put on the desk, on purpose



None of it is magic. It’s all context management.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
Micro-Check
The AI cites a journal article that doesn’t exist. Which layer failed?



The Model Layer — the brain guessed. Ground it in a real source and verify (later, with NotebookLM).

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Shift

You don’t need a “chat bot.” You need a capable assistant you can delegate to.



Don’t ask: “Write an email about the meeting.”
Delegate: “Act as a thesis advisor. Draft a recap email to my student from these notes. Highlight the revisions due before the next committee.”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Framework


R — Role: Who should the AI be?


I — Instructions: What exactly should it do? (format, length, tone)


C — Context: What information does it need?


E — Examples: Show it what “good” looks like.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
R — Role

Who should the AI be?



A patient teaching assistant
A peer reviewer for a journal
A curriculum committee chair
A grant-proposal editor



The role shapes the AI’s vocabulary, perspective, and priorities.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
I — Instructions

What exactly should it do?


Bundle the task with its format, length, and tone:


“Draft a 150-word feedback note to the student. Encouraging but specific. Use a bulleted ‘What to fix next’ list.”










Pro move


Add: “If anything is unclear, ask me before you write.”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
C — Context

What information does it need?


The “brain dump” — paste your notes, the rubric, the draft, the syllabus.








This is the same context from the two layers


You’re loading the pages onto the brain’s desk. No context = the brain guesses.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
E — Examples

Show it what “good” looks like.


Don’t just describe the output — paste one sample. The AI copies its structure, tone, and length.


“Match this style: ‘Dear Sara, strong progress this week. Three things to tighten before we meet: …’”










One example beats a paragraph


A single sample teaches more than ten lines of rules.

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Formula

“Act as a [Role]. Your job is to [Instructions]. Here is the [Context]. Match this [Example].”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The Messy Notes

What you actually scribbled after the committee meeting:


“Met Sara re: thesis ch.3. Stats section weak — needs effect sizes, not just p-values. Lit review missing 2 key papers (ask her to add). Committee wants revised draft in 3 weeks. She’s nervous about the defense — reassure. Reminder: ethics form still not submitted.”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
The RICE Prompt

Role: Act as a supportive thesis advisor.
Instructions: Draft a warm, clear follow-up email to my student. Use headers — Summary, Required Revisions, Deadline, Admin. Put the deadline in bold. End on an encouraging note. If anything is missing, add a “Questions for me” section.
Context: Notes from today’s committee meeting on Chapter 3: [paste notes]
Example: Match this opening — “Dear Sara, good progress this week. Here’s where we landed: …”

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
text:
What Made It Work

Role → wrote as a mentor, not a robot
Instructions → clear sections + tone + the “Questions for me” rule
Context → messy notes were enough — the AI extracted the structure
Example → matched the warm, personal opening

title: How AI Works & Writing Great Prompts
section: Slow It Down — Especially on Numbers
text:
Slow It Down — Especially on Numbers

By default AI answers fast and shallow — risky on grades, totals, and data.



Double-check: have it solve the same task 2–3 times — match = trust, mismatch = flag.

“Total these 40 exam scores three times. If all three match, output ‘Verified’; if not, ‘Manual Review Needed’.” — industry term: Self-Consistency.





Two more nudges for harder calls: “think step by step” (Chain of Thought — logic) · “debate it out” (Tree of Thoughts — judgment).

Delegate, don’t ask — brief the AI with RICE (Role, Instructions, Context, Examples)
